title: Haven't you lived?
hookLine: "I've done nothing today." What, haven't you lived? (Essays 3.13)

lines: THE SAME FIVE ITEMS ON THE LIST.
cards: Ten-forty at night. The list on the fridge has the same five items it had at breakfast. The inbox is still full.
And there's a sentence people say at that hour, out loud or under their breath: I did nothing today. Montaigne heard it too, and wrote it down in the essay called Of experience.
He answered with a question so short it almost sounds rude. What, haven't you lived? He doesn't ask what got finished.

teach.b: First, the complaint. Montaigne calls us great fools, himself included. We say of someone, he spent his life in idleness.
We say of ourselves, I've done nothing today. Second, his answer. Haven't you lived?
Living isn't a gap between the real tasks, he says.
It's the basic work, and the most excellent of all your occupations. Third, the excuse he hears next. If only I'd been given great affairs, people say, I'd have shown what I could do.
Montaigne turns it around. Have you known how to think about your life and manage it? Then you've done the greatest work there is.

Our job is to compose our character, not to compose books. The great and glorious masterpiece is to live fittingly. Everything else, ruling, piling up money, building, he calls little add-ons and props at most.
And notice who's saying it: a man composing a book at that very moment. He isn't against work. He's against the ledger that only counts the work.

teach.h: THE MEAL, THE TALK, THE LIGHT.
teach.b: You ate a meal. You talked someone through a bad hour. You noticed the light on the wall at four o'clock.
You were tired, and patient anyway. None of that goes on the list on the fridge.

teach.h: THE MASTERPIECE IS TO LIVE FITTINGLY.
teach.b: In Montaigne's book, it's the masterpiece.

how: Readers of Montaigne often return to this passage from Of experience as a counterweight to measuring a day only by what got finished; some keep it as a short line to say at night.

o: a scolding for wasting the day on idle pleasures
Montaigne's reply to I did nothing today: living is the work
a question asking if you've traveled far enough yet

games.q: inside haven't you lived: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne says our job is to compose books
he says our job is to compose our character, not books.
he answers I've done nothing today with a question
Montaigne includes himself among the fools who say it
he says we are great fools, and he doesn't leave himself out.

games.q: someone tells Montaigne: if only I'd been given great affairs, I'd have shown what I could do. what does he answer?
o: then go and find great affairs.
have you known how to think about and manage your life? that's the greatest work.
great affairs are for kings, not for you.
games.why: he turns the excuse around: if you've managed your own life well, you've done the greatest work there is.

practice: Go back through today, or yesterday if it's early, not by tasks but by moments: somewhere you woke, something you ate, a voice you heard, a moment you were kind or tried to be. Don't grade any of them.
Set each one down like a coin on a table, and let the pile be what it is.

wordCard.voice: Haven't you lived? Montaigne's answer to the person who says I've done nothing today: living is the basic work, and living fittingly is the masterpiece. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French, in the essay Of experience: what, haven't you lived?

carryVoice: Your line: haven't I lived. The list on the fridge was never the whole count. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 3.13, Of experience (the complaint 'I have done nothing today'; 'what, have you not lived?'; living as the most excellent occupation; to compose our character, not books; the masterpiece is to live fittingly; ruling, hoarding and building as little appendages and props)
